How many correct guesses would convince you?

Out of 10, choose a score that feels unusually good.

This is a test of evidence for better-than-chance prediction, not a test that can prove supernatural powers.

01 / State the question before seeing data

Two explanations. One experiment.

Let q be the person's true probability of a correct prediction on a trial—not the fraction correct in just 10 guesses.

Null hypothesis · Our reference model

H0: q = 0.50

No predictive advantage.

The person is as accurate as chance. Correct and incorrect predictions are equally likely.

It does not say every set of 10 guesses must contain exactly 5 correct answers.
Alternative hypothesis · What we look for

Ha: q > 0.50

A better-than-chance advantage.

The person has a success probability above 50%. High scores are the evidence we are looking for.

This is a one-sided test. Very low scores do not support this alternative.
Think, then revealSomeone gets 8 out of 10 correct. Does that mean their true q is exactly 0.80?
No. The observed proportion is 8/10 = 0.80, but it varies from experiment to experiment. The hypotheses concern the underlying q, which we do not know.
Model assumptions and an optional technical detail

We use independent trials with the same probability q of a correct prediction. Under the chance model, X, the number correct, follows Binomial(n, 0.50). For a broader one-sided null q ≤ 0.50, q = 0.50 is the boundary that gives the largest right-tail false-positive probability. The main lesson uses the simple chance null q = 0.50.

Concepts: NIST [2]; exact binomial test [3].

05 / Evidence from data versus a decision rule

The p-value comes from the data. α comes from the plan.

Keep the score fixed. Compare decision rules that could have been chosen before the experiment.

Observed data → p-value

Changing α does not change the p-value for these fixed data and this fixed test.

Decision rule

Reject H₀ if p ≤ α.

Which scores trigger rejection?

What α controls

The rule is designed so that the probability of rejecting a true H₀ is no greater than α.

Actual false-positive probability here

With only 11 possible scores, an exact binomial test cannot usually hit the chosen α exactly. Its actual error rate can be smaller.

Design comparison only: moving this control after seeing a result is not permission to change the original study's cutoff. The live experiment keeps its locked α.

Type I error: a false alarm.

A false positive: the test flags something that is not there.

A decision can be wrong even when the test was used correctly.

Type I error rate
= P(reject H₀ | H₀ is true)

Exact long-run rate for this rule

An error is an event. An error rate describes repeated use of a procedure. Neither tells us the probability that a particular real-world conclusion is wrong.

CheckDoes α = 0.05 mean this exact 10-guess test must make 50 false alarms in every 1,000 studies?
No. The actual error probability can be below α, and the number of false alarms also fluctuates randomly. At n = 10 and α = 0.05, the exact rate is 1.0742%, or about 11 per 1,000 on average.
07 / Repeated studies when an advantage is real

Type II error: missing a real advantage.

A visual analogy first. Then use the coin-flip simulation to connect reality with the test decision.

Different example · Same logic

State the null before naming the error.

H₀ Not pregnantHₐ Pregnant

The doctor says “You’re not pregnant!” In this hypothetical example, the person is pregnant. Which part of the decision is wrong?

Reality
PregnantH₀ is false.
Test conclusion
“You’re not pregnant!”Maps to failing to reject H₀.
False H₀ + fail to reject H₀ = Type II error.
A false negative: the test misses something that is there.

Back to our coin test: A real advantage exists (q = 0.70), but the test fails to reject H₀. A nonsignificant result does not prove no advantage.

Now imagine a simulated forecaster whose true q is 0.70. For the next examples, use n = 10 and α = 0.05.

“Fail to reject H₀” does not mean “H₀ is true.” A real advantage may not produce enough evidence in a small study.

The 70% forecaster is a hypothetical success-probability model for teaching power. We are not making a claim that someone can foresee an independent fair coin. q is not the coin's probability of heads.

Exact power at q = 0.70

Power = P(reject H₀ | q = 0.70)

Power = 1 − β

Here, β is the probability of failing to reject H₀ when q really is 0.70.

Power is not the probability that Hₐ is true. It is a property of a test at a specified true alternative.

Why does power occasionally dip when n increases by one?

The exact binomial rejection cutoff moves in whole numbers. When it jumps up by one, power can dip briefly. Larger samples improve power overall, not necessarily at every single increment of n. Lower α makes rejection harder or leaves the cutoff unchanged; increasing true q makes detection easier. Power is computed from the chosen alternative q, not from the observed sample's success fraction.

Important: the displayed formula assumes independent tests and uses the actual per-test error rate, 11/1024. Students predicting the same shared coin sequence need not have independent scores, so do not automatically apply this number to that classroom setup.

12 / Take the logic with you

Seven ideas. One coherent experiment.

H₀The reference claim: the predictor performs at chance, q = 0.50.
HₐThe target alternative: the predictor does better than chance, q > 0.50.
p-valueUnder H₀, the probability of the observed score or a higher score.
αA prechosen threshold controlling the long-run probability of rejecting a true H₀.
Type IReject H₀ when it is true: a false alarm.
Type IIFail to reject H₀ when the specified alternative is true: a miss.
PowerThe probability of rejecting H₀ at a specified true alternative. Power = 1 − β; it depends on the design and the true effect.
Exit ticket

Finish these two sentences.

“A p-value of 0.0107 means…”
“An experiment can miss a real advantage because…”

The challenge

Lesson guide

Using the coin-flip lab

Designed for an introductory biostatistics class. Use a projector for whole-class discussion, or let students open their own copy for independent practice.

Setup and controls

Open this file directly in a browser. No internet or installation is required. Use the Back/Next buttons or ←/→ keys; arrow keys keep their normal behavior while a control has focus. F toggles fullscreen where supported. The Guide menu contains all references. On the Type I and Type II error pages, use “Picture the error” and “Try the coin experiment” to switch views; “Reveal the reasoning” explains the meme. “New round” clears the live round without a browser popup, keeps the selected coin mode and α, and offers Undo until a new prediction or setting is entered. Large type improves projection but may require scrolling on smaller displays.

This is a local, single-user learning activity, not a polling server. It does not collect student responses. Students can save a text summary on the final screen. Reloading resets the current work. Simulated coin flips are pseudorandom; all reported theoretical probabilities are computed exactly from binomial probabilities, subject only to floating-point arithmetic.

Key distinctions

q vs p-value: q is a data-generating success probability, not a tail area. α vs actual size: at n = 10 and α = 0.05, reject only for 9 or 10 correct; the actual Type I error rate is 11/1024 = 1.0742%, not 5%. Power vs “truth probability”: power is conditional on a specified alternative. At q = 0.70 it is 14.9308% for that same test. Fail to reject vs accept: absence of statistical significance does not establish no advantage.

Scope of the simulations

Each binomial experiment assumes a fixed n, independent trials, and a common q. Simulations of multiple experiments are independent. Live scores from students predicting a single shared coin sequence may be dependent. The power lab's q = 0.70 is hypothetical: it generates correct/incorrect outcomes and does not alter the fair coin's heads probability or establish psychic ability. The lesson uses a prespecified right-tailed exact test and does not test for below-chance performance.

References and calculation notes

[1] American Statistical Association (2016). Statement on statistical significance and p-values. Supports the cautions about interpreting p-values as probabilities of hypotheses and about treating significance as a substitute for scientific reasoning.
ASA statement and principles · DOI of the full statement: 10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108.

[2] NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, §7.1.3. “What are statistical tests?” Background for null/alternative hypotheses, prespecified decision rules, and the two types of error.
NIST hypothesis-testing reference

[3] R Core Team. Documentation for stats::binom.test, “Exact Binomial Test.” The lesson uses the “greater” alternative with null probability 0.50.
Official R documentation

Original calculations. p(x) = P(X ≥ x | q = 0.50). Let c be the smallest integer with p(c) ≤ α. The actual Type I error rate is P(X ≥ c | q = 0.50); power at q₁ > 0.50 is P(X ≥ c | q = q₁); β = 1 − power. If no score satisfies the cutoff, the rejection set is empty. Counts are converted to exact binomial probabilities without a normal approximation.
